reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AASLD
clinicalPearls: Presents typically in childhood or young adulthood with features of portal hypertension despite relatively preserved hepatocellular function
Variceal bleeding and splenomegaly are common presenting features, often with normal or only mildly deranged liver enzymes
The characteristic combination is presinusoidal portal hypertension with well-maintained synthetic liver function
Strongly associated with autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease, so renal involvement should always be assessed
May overlap with Caroli disease, and the two together are termed Caroli syndrome
Ascending cholangitis can occur when there is coexisting bile duct ectasia
Liver biopsy shows broad bands of mature fibrous tissue containing abnormal, sometimes dilated, bile duct profiles reflecting the ductal plate malformation
Management centres on controlling variceal bleeding and portal hypertension, treating cholangitis, and monitoring associated renal disease
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital hepatic fibrosis is a developmental disorder arising from malformation of the embryonic ductal plate, the template from which the intrahepatic bile ducts form. Defective remodelling, frequently due to mutations in ciliary genes such as PKHD1, leaves persistent, abnormally shaped bile duct structures embedded within expanding portal fibrous tissue. The fibrosis is broad-based and located within and around portal tracts, obstructing portal venous flow at a presinusoidal level and producing portal hypertension. Because the hepatic parenchyma and sinusoids are relatively spared, hepatocellular synthetic function is generally maintained, distinguishing it from cirrhosis. The same ciliopathy commonly affects the kidneys, explaining the frequent association with polycystic kidney disease.
additionalInvestigations: Liver biopsy demonstrating portal fibrosis with ductal plate malformation and preserved parenchyma
Ultrasound and cross-sectional imaging of liver, spleen, and portal system
Renal imaging to detect associated polycystic or fibrocystic kidney disease
Upper endoscopy to screen for and grade oesophagogastric varices
Genetic testing where a ciliopathy syndrome is suspected
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography if biliary ectasia or cholangitis is suspected
redFlags: Acute variceal haemorrhage requiring urgent endoscopic and haemodynamic management
Cholangitis with sepsis in those with coexisting bile duct ectasia
Progressive renal impairment from associated kidney disease
Rapidly enlarging spleen with worsening cytopenias
reference.prognosis: The hepatic outlook is often favourable because liver function is preserved and complications of portal hypertension are usually manageable; overall prognosis is influenced substantially by the severity of associated renal disease and, where present, recurrent cholangitis.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the condition as cirrhosis and giving an unduly pessimistic prognosis
Failing to screen for and manage varices before a first bleed
Not recognising overlap with Caroli disease and the attendant cholangitis and malignancy risks
